newsitem.title: USA: FTC gets autoparts database merger antitrust pact.
newsitem.headline: FTC gets autoparts database merger antitrust pact.

text.p: The Federal Trade Commission said Wednesday that Cooperative Computing Inc, a leading provider of computerized autoparts databases, has agreed to divestiture before acquiring a competitor in a proposed settlement that would resolve competition concerns.
The FTC said that absent relief, Cooperative's proposed acquisition of Triad Systems Corp would substantially lessen competition in the development and sale of electronic parts catalogs.
It said the merger would likely result in increased prices and reduced services in violation of antitrust laws.

To resolve FTC concerns, the proposed settlement would require Cooperative, upon completion of the merger, to divest through an exclusive, royalty-free and perpetual license, its electronics parts catalog to MacDonald Computer Systems or another FTC-approved buyer.
The agency in its complaint said Cooperative and Triad are two of only three firms that develop and sell electronics parts catalogs.

These databases index and list more than a million new automotive replacement parts and are used primarily by independent warehouse distributors and jobbers providing parts to mechanics and other installers.

Cooperative, of Austin, Texas, is a privately-held firm that offers software products for tracking auto parts inventory. It has developed and marketed with its software a proprietary database of domestic and foreign auto parts.
Triad, of Livermore, Calif., offers applications software for efficiency in automotive parts businesses. It also develops and sells a proprietary database of domestic and foreign auto parts.
MacDonald is a California-based private firm that has developed and sold autoparts inventory management systems, recently integrated with an electronic parts catalog licensed from Triad.

The FTC voted 5-0 to approve the proposed consent agreement. An analysis of the agreement will be published in the Federal Register and subject to 60-day public comment period. The FTC will then decide whether to make it final.
If Cooperative failed in the divestiture, it would be required to divest to another FTC-approved acquirer within 60 days after the date on which the consent order was made final.

A consent agreement is for settlement purposes only and does not constitute an admission of a law violation. When the FTC issues a consent order on a final basis, it carries the force of law with respect to future actions, the FTC said.
